newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Filipino activists to invite anti-APEC speakers.
newsitem.headline: Filipino activists to invite anti-APEC speakers.

text.p: A group opposed to the APEC regional forum said on Wednesday they planned to invite controversial outside speakers to a meeting in the Philippines despite a previous rebuff from President Fidel Ramos.

Organisers of the "Manila People's Forum on APEC" (MPFA) said they would invite a "high official" of the East Timorese resistance movement and an Indonesian dissident to attend their November 21-23 meeting just before the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum on November 25 at Subic Bay.
Ramos earlier barred the entry of Nobel peace prize laureate Jose Ramos-Horta on grounds his presence in Manila this month might disrupt APEC.
In lieu of Ramos-Horta, MPFA organisers said they had invited another "high official" of the East Timorese resistance movement and possibly four other resistance members.
Dissident Indonesian academic George Aditjondro, now exiled in Australia, had also been invited, MPFA's Walden Bello said.
The group is opposed to APEC's policies in favor of liberalising trade on the grounds workers will lose wages and the environment will suffer.

"Our delegates...are not threats to national security and we fully expect the Philippine government not to bar their entry," Bello told a news conference. "We will be able to test this ban in the next few days."
Bello described Aditjondro as a scholar who "is by no means anybody who can be classified as a terrorist except in the eyes of the Indonesian government".
He refused to identify the East Timorese resistance leader, saying, "We want to make sure this person can enter the country but we can assure you this person will be there."
Indonesian President Suharto is among the leaders of 18 APEC member economies expected to attend the summit.
Indonesia invaded East Timor, a former Portuguese colony in 1975, and annexed it the following year in a move never recognised by the United Nations.
Bello said some of the East Timorese they had invited would come from Kuala Lumpur where Malaysian human rights groups planned to hold a three-day meeting on East Timor starting on November 9.
Organisers of the Kuala Lumpur meeting said on Tuesday they were going ahead with their conference, defying government pressure to cancel the meeting.
